utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning to you, Madam Registrar, could you please call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, Accused Nikolic is still not with us today. For the record also he has filed a declaration whereby, as confirmed by Ms. Nikolic earlier on, he waives his right to be present and accepts the proceedings to continue, provided his counsel is here, and she is. From the Defence teams I think it is Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic who are still not with us. Prosecution is Mr. Thayer and Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Thank you. Yes, we are sitting today in -- pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge Stole is not present. He will be present with us hopefully Monday if he's feeling better. We agreed yesterday that we would maintain sort of three items on the agenda for today. One of which we are expecting to hear the end results of the either examination of the video or discussions that you may have had. I'm referring to the two-hour or half an hour video. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we were relieved to discover that the unedited version of the video was in fact only about 20 minutes long. The Chamber will be even more relieved to know that we are not asking that that version be played. We are content that the edited version is played to the Chamber. As I respectfully suggested yesterday, we would invite the Chamber to view that video and then we would have some short submissions as to its admissibility in due course. Could I just say this: I mentioned this to my learned friend Mr. McCloskey. We would invite the Chamber to say in fact the Prosecution should go first at that point and explain why they say it is admissable, pursuant to Rule 89, and then we could make our objections thereafter. That, we would suggest, is the more logical way of approaching this particular problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My suggestion to you, if my colleagues agree, is to start then first with Stefanie Frease's testimony. Do you have problems? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, I think we're ready to proceed. We just need to ensure the presence of the witness who is on her way down. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then in the meantime I think we can proceed with watching this video and I don't know who wishes to respond to Mr. Josse's remarks or submissions on admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Everyone. Yes, Mr. Josse did speak to me about this, this morning, and we are fine on that. I would like to give you a -- I think it would be helpful to give you a brief background of the video so that it will help you in understanding its relevance, though I don't think you need hear much for me, frankly. It speaks for itself. And I have been invited to speak by Defence counsel in any event, so if I could just say a few words about that. We had had the order differently, but I think we can adjust to this order without a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Listen, if -- I suggest starting first with Ms. Frease's testimony because in reality I don't know how long she will be testifying, and I mean I would rather have her finish her testimony first without having it interrupted or given in two separate sittings. But if this disturbs your programme, I mean we can easily accommodate you. I mean it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're -- I think we're adjusting fine to that. I always look to Ms. Stewart to see how we are with -- one issue -- one of the things that we wanted to show you with Ms. Frease were just the UHER machine and -- and the tapes, have her talk about a bit. Then we need to take a break to move the them into the booth where they plug them in so you can get the best sound quality and actually play the original tape. So we just need a five or 10-minute break because if you will recall, lining up old reel-to-reel tapes is not as easy as digital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That convinces me that the suggestion to start with Stefanie Frease I think is the best one, so that we go through the whole process and conclude it first. But, if in the meantime we can see this video, until she -- until she comes down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no problem with the Court viewing the video and hearing the submissions sometime later today, or if need be, sometime future. I have no difficulty with that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a better approach, Mr. Josse. I think we will have time to hear submissions today as well. I understand this is a five-minute video now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. One thing I don't have for you with the video as what we had with the last one is a few stills identifying people. But that will come. But if I can just give you a brief preview of it, I think it will be helpful. This is a video that was provided to the OTP in an interview with General Zivanovic many years ago. And, as you can see from the video, it is a celebration of his departure as the commander of the Drina Corps, and General Krstic is coming on. And you will see a reference in some of the speeches that it is now General Krstic who is the commander and General Zivanovic has gone. Now, this is a very important issue, so that you understand who was in command at the time of the key events. And you will see other evidence that I won't go into now, about precisely when General Krstic took over command. And so on that important issue, as it -- as you -- as you already have seen, we have an intercept between -- we believe between General Krstic and Accused Borovcanin on the 13th, and it's -- it's at a time when General Krstic, in our belief, is commander. So this is an issue that this has relevance to. I think more importantly it gives you a real inside view into -- into part of the Main Staff, because what you'll see is General Maric arrives on that big field, you will recall, from this restaurant we went to see, the yellow restaurant. He arrives in a helicopter. He is greeted by -- I believe it's General Milovanovic his Chief of Staff, who you have not seen before and may not recognise. We'll point him out so that you understand who he is. And you'll see how they sit next to each other. General -- General Milovanovic at the table with General Gvero next to him and then General Maric is arriving. You have Mladic, Milovanovic, Gvero, and these are important issues, where people sit at these sorts of parties, and I think it's an important thing for you to see how these top generals relate to each other, how they sit. There's very few of them. And -- and it's a July -- I believe 21st, I always get it mixed up with the 20th or 21st, but these are just, you know, right in the middle of these events, just after the mass executions have taken place. So these are some of the reasons why we believe it's relevant. And it is -- we have a transcript for it, which is PO2044. And the video clip itself is PO2046. And the video is subtitled, so I -- and it's not the best -- it's that subtitling that's a little below the screen, but I would ....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the number of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The -- 2044 is the transcript, and the clip is 2046, which does have the -- the subtitling, and this is an edited version, as Mr. Josse has told you. We just tried to pick out the parts that had had most relevance to the case. And I don't -- if -- we don't really neat the booth to get involved in this, I think it would be just better if we hear the B/C/S and try to follow the transcript. We had -- we've got hard copy transcripts coming down, but they haven't got here yet, which obviously is the ideal way, but if you look at the transcripts you sort of lose the video, so ... I guess we have e-court and the video, so if someone can keep the transcript going in e-court. So I guess we're ready to go, and if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I may pause it a time or two just to identify someone, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll try again, but you probably recognised General Krstic, General Zivanovic and hopefully the sound will come back to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still no sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We played this with sound last night, the same machine, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This has happened before. Is Ms. Frease around? Yeah. Then shall we start with Ms. Frease or shall we give this another try? They are on their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is Milovanovic in the -- looking at his watch right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is Generals Milovanovic and Gvero sitting at the table

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you wish to make submissions? Mr. Josse? By the way, is it Yosse or Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Josse. The Prosecution submit that this is relevant to the command issue between Generals Zivanovic and General Krstic. Your Honour, I'm bound to say there is not very much I, on behalf of General Gvero, can say about that. That is an issue which doesn't concern the Defence of General Gvero in the slightest. And if it be an issue in the case, then the Court must take what course it feels appropriate in relation to this video. And I wasn't aware that my learned friends were deploying that as an argument for the admissibility for this particular piece of footage. However, perhaps more important in relation to our case is his second assertion. And really what he says is that it's important for the Chamber to know, "Where people sit at these sort of parties." And in our submission, really, it takes the matter no further at all. It's irrelevant. Where do people sit, they sit across the table, as this Chamber saw, looking at that very video. It's of no probative value whatsoever in that regard, and we would suggest to the Court that so far as General Gvero is concerned, this -- my learned friends are trying to put this piece of evidence in as a piece of pure prejudice. In effect guilt by association. It's classic in that regard. We'd also make one other remark in passing and that's this: The events we saw on the video occurred in the municipality of Sokolac. They are not covered by the indictment. They are not near, certainly relatively speaking, the events of Srebrenica, and in our submission that's another reason to illustrate why the events on the video are irrelevant. But, Your Honour, I repeat, if the video is admitted purely in order to go to the issue of command between Generals Krstic and Zivanovic, then, notwithstanding I haven't had a chance to discuss it directly with General Gvero, that's something clearly we couldn't possibly object to. It's the second ground that we say is wholly prejudicial, irrelevant, and doesn't fall within Rule 89. The issue is really as simply that, is there any probative value in it at all, is it relevant, and is it prejudicial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is prejudicial, it's meant to be prejudicial, that's why we -- it is relevant evidence to prejudice this in that it shows that he is part of the Main Staff, that he is with General Mladic at a key time. He is the one person we see on the video that is telling the group where General Mladic is and makes an inference on what he is doing at a time when we have some over 7.000 Muslims in their graves a few days old. That -- I don't think anyone will suggest here that it was not General Mladic that was one -- the main force behind this. Yes, it is meant to be prejudicial. That is why it is so relevant. And that General Gvero was the one that's giving the toast and saying what he is saying. Yes, it is prejudicial. That's why we are offering it. I would also point out what General Mladic had to say, he does make reference to Srebrenica and what had been done in Srebrenica at a time when he knows exactly what he has done, and they're all sitting there smiling, knowing what they have done and what they will continue to do in the woods as the days go on. And there is one word that Mladic mentions about Serbs disappearing. You'll here other evidence that this is the propaganda, the call to arms from the beginning of this war that the Serbs repeat over and over again, that the Muslims are coming to commit genocide on the Serbs. It's the -- and they -- we must prevent that so the Serbs do not disappear. Well, this is the same word or close to it, that he used just a few days earlier to Mr. Mandic, "Mr. Mandic it's up to you whether your people survivor disappear." So this video is relevant in a number of ways. Does it answer the questions that you have to resolve? No, it doesn't. But does it help? Yes, it does. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, two or three comments. First of all, of course for what it's worth in this regard, it's worth a great deal generally, my client is not charged in relation to the mass murder. Secondly, there is no dispute whatsoever that General Gvero was a member of the Main Staff. There is an enormous amount of evidence to prove that, and this Chamber will see no attempt by the Defence of General Gvero to show otherwise. What we ask rhetorically is how does the video advance the case against General Gvero in a material way, and that we would respectfully say is a test you should apply in deciding whether it is admissable against him in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is that we would rather -- if we are to admit the video, we would rather admit the entire video rather than part of it, which has been edited by one of the parties. So that is the first point that we'd like to make. So if that will be the case, would you have anything to add to your submissions that you have already made? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just ask about the logistics of that? Does the Chamber want the whole video played in open court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We want to have the whole video available. So that at the end of the day we admit the video we will admit the whole video and not parts which have been edited by the Prosecution from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, could I just emphasise, as I hope I made clear first this morning, that the Defence have no difficulty with the edited video being admitted. My slight concern is this, Your Honour: If the Court is going to decide whether to admit the whole video, then surely the Court is going to need to view the whole video before making that decision as to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You got it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we suggest is the following, so that we don't take much time, which we need for other things this morning: That you make this video available for the Trial Chamber, and then we will come back to you on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think, with respect, that's wise for this reason: The reason I needed to turn to Mr. Krgovic, besides the fact he is my lead counsel, is the fact that he really viewed it because it was only in his language, the whole video. The whole video didn't have the subtitles upon it, so therefore I have to bow to his judgement in that regard. If the Chamber is going to view it, then clearly arrangements are going to need to be made for the whole of it to be translated and transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have the transcript of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the transcript of the whole video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the whole video. And this is the main reason why, basically -- not one of the reasons, not necessarily the main reason, one of the reasons why we need the whole video. First of all, the way Mr. McCloskey approached it, although he was inviting us, and not giving us instructions, was to sort of don't bother much with the transcript, because if you look at the transcript you will miss what the visual side of it, and that is -- that is true. But if we have the transcript available, and the whole video available, and all the time that we need to view the video carefully, then we can place ourselves in a better position to make an assessment of your submissions and of Mr. McCloskey's submission and come back with a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To make our position plain, Your Honour, Mr. Krgovic advises me that we have no problem with that, whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So it's up to you to make now -- make this video available at the earliest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think that's an excellent idea. I want to make sure we have the whole transcript. I'm not sure we've given you the entire transcript, but we will endeavour to do that. As you can see, it's hard to transcribe these sorts of things, but -- but we'll get that to you. Because I think you're right, it's good to view the video, but then it's good to study the transcript and the words, what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that disposes of the first item on the agenda, and I thank you, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Josse, for your very constructive approach in discussing this matter. Can we bring in Ms. Frease? All right. Judge Kwon is suggesting -- one moment, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Kwon is suggesting that we dispose of the other issue on the agenda, the one relating to Rupert Smith, the two motions, the Gvero and Miletic motions. And then we have a break, you have the time to prepare the equipment for Ms. Frease, and then we can continue and finish with Ms. Frease. All right? Have you decided, will Mr. Josse go first? One moment. Give me a few seconds, Mr. Josse, to get my documents right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, when it became clear that the Chamber had a little time today we considered that this might be a constructive item to make a few submissions about. We of course were not aware as to whether the Chamber had started examining this matter at all or in any detail, but felt that some clarification was worthwhile because to some extent the Chamber may feel that the filings in this matter have become, I would suggest slightly confused and slightly bogged down in what we submit is actually a rather straightforward matter. I could, if the Chamber required, go through listing the various filings there have been in relation to this matter. I don't know whether that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have this them all here. That's why I told you give me two seconds, so that I organised them at least in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I won't do that. Safe to say there've been two from General Gvero's Defence, two from General Miletic's Defence and I think two from the Prosecution. There should be six filings in relation to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Chamber will observe what we stated in the last paragraph of our filing of the 15th of December, that we had felt compelled to file the matter confidentially. All subsequent filings I note were filed confidentially, and we have explained the reason in the filing, which I won't repeat in open session. But I think the matter can safely be discussed in open session now, notwithstanding the fact that all these filings were confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are of the same opinion, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, the questions we would invite the Chamber to consider as follows: Firstly, has the Prosecution complied with Rule 94 bis (a) in relation to the purported expert evidence of General Smith? If they have not, then we would invite the Chamber, one, so to rule. Then to in effect give directions as to when and how the Chamber should so comply. We would suggest that for the Prosecution to realistically comply with that rule, they need, as they have for other experts, to serve a notice under Rule 94 bis (a) to provide a translation and stopping there, that is no longer an issue, a translation I'm glad to say was provided yesterday. And thirdly, we would submit that what the Prosecution really need to do is to explain in their notice why they say this gentleman is an expert witness and why he is suitable as an expert witness. We submit strongly that realistically the burden is on them to show that he should be an expert and is an expert, and thereafter that triggers a response from the Defence under Rule 94 bis (b) as to why the Defence say he is not suitable to be an expert. By way of particular and stark example in this case, we would say that an obvious failure of the Prosecution is the fact that they haven't provided a curriculum vitae for the general. Now, of course, we know a fair amount about his background, it would be churlish of me to suggest otherwise. However, the Prosecution, we submit, need to demonstrate more clearly and carefully why in particular they say he is capable of being an expert in relation to the Main Staff of the VRS. Having said all of that, were the Chamber to decide that the Prosecution have complied with Rule 92 bis (a), then we would still ask for some further directions to allow the Defence to respond fully under 94 bis (b). And Your Honour, we are grateful to the Prosecution, because we contend that they concede as much, if I could be given a moment. In their filing of the 2nd of January, 2007, and I'm sure I can read this bit out in open session. At paragraph 6 they say, and it's right to say that in that filing they oppose strongly the submissions I have hitherto made, they say, "Nevertheless to the extent any of the accused may seek additional time in order to more fully respond pursuant to Rule 94 bis (b), the Prosecution would have no objection to such a request." So I repeat, if the Court is against the primarily submission that we make, then nonetheless we would still ask some direction as to how the matter should proceed. We would then realise the burden, in effect, was on us under 94 bis (B) as to why we say the general should not be an expert. In short what no one is asking at this stage, as I understand it, is for the Court to determine whether General Smith is an expert. I have no doubt that day will come, and for better or for worse, this Chamber will be burdened with that particular problem, but not at the moment. In effect, we're asking for the Court simply to give some directions and some guidance before we proceed further. And I repeat what I said when I began, we had some concerns that these various filings didn't make that altogether clear and were starting to wrap the two issues up together, and at this stage we haven't got that far. Finally, one thing for the Chamber's information, which is of importance certainly to us. We learnt yesterday that General Smith is going to be a factual witness in the case of Dragomir Milosevic, a trial which I'm sure this Chamber is aware has just started. So we suspect he will give evidence as a fact-based witness in that case first and then give evidence in this Chamber thereafter. He has, of course, given evidence here before, as I am sure the Chamber is aware. Unless I can assist further, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose we should hear your submissions, Madam Fauveau, and then give the floor to Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was following.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief. I will be very brief. I join all the submissions of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. I think the issue really fundamentally boils down this morning to at what point was proper notice under 94 bis given for the purpose of tolling any response by Defence counsel. And I think we -- that's where we need to focus, because that's the most important thing, to get the ball moving ahead, as opposed to spending time trying to extricate ourselves from what's happened. Certainly we could have simplified matters had we, back in November, when we disclosed this expert report, slapped a 94 bis label on the disclosure transmittal correspondence when we did so. That would have, I think, solved our issue. That didn't happen, unfortunately, so here we are. I think we need to put in context though, in terms of answering some of these questions about whether 94 bis has, in fact, been complied with. In you look at our filing of 2 January, this has been a very straightforward endeavour with respect to General Smith. Our position has been clear and simple from the beginning as early as March of 2006, when Mr. McCloskey made it clear on the record that we are offering General Smith as both a fact witness with respect to Zepa, as well as an expert witness with respect to certain command issues, but more fundamentally with respect to the importance of a Main Staff. That position has been repeated on the record on no fewer than two occasions or at least one other occasion, supplemented obviously by our 65 ter witness summary of General Smith, which again repeated our intent to offer his testimony as both a Zepa fact witness, and the expert witness that Mr. McCloskey had described previously. Therefore, when the disclosure was made in November of 2006, as soon as you click on the document and it pops up and it says, "Expert statement of sir General Rupert Smith," our position, respectfully, Your Honours, that Rule 94 bis has been complied with at that point. It is unambiguous, the purpose for which it is being offered. It is consistent with what we have been advising Defence counsel for months. And the question ends there, as far as we're concerned. Now, again, certainly we concede that had we slapped 94 bis, maybe some extra bells would have gone off and we wouldn't be in the position we're in. We believe that doing that, given what we had alerted counsel to already, was sufficient compliance, and there's certainly nothing explicit in 94 bis, much less anything implicit in 94 bis, which requires the Prosecution to do so. Certainly it would be a preferred practice to have sent perhaps a separate notification or submission with respect to that, but we did what we did, we thought that that would be sufficient, given -- given all the circumstances and we still respectfully submit that that was a reasonable course of action and that -- that it is a very simple and straightforward issue that's before the Court with respect to whether 94 bis has been complied with. We did not concede, as my learned friend has represented, that we did not comply with 94 bis in our 2 January 2007 filing. What we did acknowledge was that there is confusion that has been created and that, should Defence counsel require more time, should the Court decide to toll the issue at any time of its choosing, including this moment, we have no objection to that. We are not -- as the Court is aware, we are not procedural absolutists on this side. So along with the fact that General Smith's testimony will not occur most likely until sometime in the fall of 2007, possibly later, but that's sort of what we have in mind, given how we're breaking up the tour of this trial, I would just leave it in the Court's hands at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fall of 2007. Did the Prosecution not say that it would expect it -- their case to be concluded before summer of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Judge Kwon. Given the reality that we're facing, I don't -- I don't see us getting to where we need to be, given the volume of testimony that we have ahead of us, as hard as everybody's working. You know, we'll -- we'll regroup, regather, and see whether we can meet that, but just -- I see Mr. McCloskey getting to his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to discuss that. You will hear news about that very soon. Yes, Mr. Josse, would you like to reply to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just this, Your Honour: First of all, I was not suggesting the Prosecution conceded that they hadn't complied. My point was a different one. Secondly, I would simply emphasise what we said in paragraph 2 of our filing of the 15th of December. My learned friend does concede that perhaps the Prosecution could have done things differently. We place great reliance on that note of the 31st of October, its juxtaposition to the events that we are presently discussing, and the fact that General Smith was not mentioned on that notice. That is essential part of our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask a question to Mr. Josse to clarify? Apart from the opposition or the issue of the procedural issue, whether Prosecution has complied with the procedural requirement and apart from the issue whether Sir Rupert has an expertise on military matters, do you also suggest that either a witness should be either a fact witness or an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We will almost certainly make that very submission. Or, at the very least we will submit that in this case it will be inappropriate for an important factual witness like Sir Rupert to then be an expert in another field of the case, because it really, we will submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I have the reason for that? Apart from the lack of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well simply because the Prosecution could choose any number of individuals who have no axe to grind, who have genuine objectivity who weren't as intimately involved in these events as their expert. I suspect in due course what we will submit to the Court is that if one looks at some of the things that General Smith is saying, he, like so many of the players in these tragic events tried to explain away, dare I use the expression, his limited role. As someone who was a player in the events, he really, we submit, is not a suitable, dispassionate, and proper expert. That's the submission we would like to develop in due course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just -- to the question of Judge Kwon. I think this was already said in my reply. We are not against the possibility that one person be a factual witness and an expert witness in certain situations. Here this is a situation where one person will be factual witness on certain aspects and at the same time expert on the role of the accused in these events, while the same person -- the person who should be an expert is -- had also a role in the events. Because of this duality, it won't be possible to separate the facts from the testimony as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Of course we reserve judgement on this. We have started working on it, by the way. So as suggested by Judge Kwon, I think we should have a break now. I think we'll give you 30 minutes by which time you should organise yourselves and have everything -- everything ready and then we will start and finish with Ms. Frease, okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you're familiar with the procedure, so we will move straight to your solemn declaration. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease. I would like to put to you a few questions, and I would -- just wanted to ask you to keep your voice up and allow a short pause between the question and answer so that the interpreters have time to catch up with what you are saying. Initially I would like to begin with some of your background. Could you tell us about your educational background first?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a masters degree from Columbia University in international affairs, and an undergraduate degree, a bachelors degree from the University of Washington on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you speak more than one language? Do you have language skills?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what languages you speak?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I speak the B/C/S language, as it's referred to here, Italian, and I'm studying French.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you have testified previously before this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that in the matter of Prosecutor against Radoslav Krstic in 2001?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Prior to that had you been in the employ of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what period that was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was from April 1995 to July of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Since July of 2000, have you held other employment?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what nature of that employment was and where you worked?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. From August of 1990 to June of 1995, I worked for the Coalition for International Justice in Washington, DC, a non-profit organisation, and I was director of programmes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And following your engagement there, did you hold any other employment?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us about that and what your duties and responsibilities were there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I worked at the International Criminal Court from June of 2005 to June of 2006 where I was responsible for setting up the field operations and investigations in Chad with respect to the Sudan Darfur case that the ICC is responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Following your engagement with the ICC, have you held any other employment up until now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. After leaving -- well, after leaving the ICC I started studying French for a couple of months, and then had a short consultancy back here with the OTP in October and November, and returned in January again for a short-term contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if I may, can I just refer you back to the time when you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor before 2001.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, after you came to work for the Office of the Prosecutor initially, were you thereafter assigned to work on the Srebrenica investigation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us in what capacity you did that work?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. I started working for the court in April of 1995 and in July of 1995 I was sent out to the field to Tuzla in mid-July 1995 to conduct preliminary investigations with -- well, we were a team of four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated previously you have an understanding of the B/C/S language, you speak, read, and write it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how would you rate your proficiency in that language?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I would say I have a very solid working knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, while you were a member of this team conducting investigations into the events of Srebrenica, did the Office of the Prosecutor acquire certain material relating to intercepted radio communications?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you become involved -- well, could you just tell us about how that material was acquired in terms of the stages it was acquired in, the type of material that was acquired?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. The Office of the Prosecutor first began to acquire that material in March of 1998 and I was involved with it really from the beginning and throughout the time that I was with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the material that you became involved with, was that a fairly large volume of material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so that the Court has a general idea, can you tell us, give us a sense of what it was like handling that material. Was that a fairly straightforward processing of it or was it labour-intensive and slow, deliberate?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It wasn't straightforward, in part because we received the material in many different batches. So we worked our way through it as we received it, and as we got to understand and know the material better, it involved looking at printed transcripts of the material and then later notebook -- notebooks, the original transcriptions of that material. After that also audiorecordings of that material and then eventually also electronic versions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, could you describe your role for the Court in terms of the processing of this intercepted material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, I was very involved with it from the beginning, and oversaw the -- its processing. Early on we put together a small team, I put together a small team of interpreters and language assistants that began to work through it and we just -- we established a system by which we could keep track of the material in a way that would be searchable and reliable. And that process also evolved as we got to know the material better. I essentially oversaw the process and worked very closely with the material for about a two-year period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you also become involved in the -- well, the analysis and organisation of that material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did -- well, could you tell us what that involved, briefly?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. It initially involved setting up a fairly simple table and then eventually, as -- as we understood the material better and saw some of the complexities of the material, we established a database that would help us make connections between the various versions of the conversations, for lack of a better term. The connections between the printouts that we had and the notebooks that we had, and then the sometimes multiple recordings of the same conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you make use of investigators, for example, in this process?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you make use of military analysis -- analysts or analyses in this process?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. People on the team were very involved with this material. We did the initial analysis, but had constant communication with the military analysts and investigators on showing how the material related to the other -- the other documents and witness statements and other information that the investigation had collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, as part of the processing of this material was that done first in relation to -- was that done in relation to your organisation of the material with regard to the case in which you testified, the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is that we -- we had the information before and we were simply working with it to understand better the events that -- that occurred in 1995. And then that body of material certainly fed into the Krstic trial and subsequent trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was one of the objectives in the processing of this material for you to determine whether or not the material was reliable or authentic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you continuing to do -- to engage in this processing in relation to the organisation of the materials with respect to this particular case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in determining whether this material was reliable and authentic, did you have an occasion to review some of the intercepted material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what kind of material you examined?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you examine printouts of these --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- intercepted communications, for example?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We examined the printouts which we had initially, then notebooks, then audiorecordings, and then electronic printouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you are aware that your testimony today is only limited to some extent and we will revisit that at some time in more detail on another occasion. But I would like to focus your attention specifically to two audiotapes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first is a tape that's designated T000-0471, otherwise known as Q2. Are you familiar with that designation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us if you know the circumstances under which that tape came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In March of 1998 there was a mission to Tuzla, to the 2 Corps headquarters, and it was during that mission that 2 Corps authorities provided access to 19 tapes. When I say that they provided access, they -- they let members of the Prosecution team observe those tapes but not take possession of the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You say this is in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know who was involved in identifying those particular tapes from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I believe it was Peter Nicholson and Richard Butler, Rick Butler. There may have been others, but -- but those two individuals come to mind. There was also a -- a gentleman by the name of Jack Hunter who the ICTY OTP team had brought in from the bureau of alcohol, tobacco and firearms from Washington, D.C., who was an expert in radio communication and tape authentication, and he also came into contact with those tapes at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that the Prosecution team did not take those tapes in March of 1998. And do you know the reason for that? Do you know why that's -- that was the case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't have proper authority at that point from the Bosnian Ministry of Defence to take possession of those materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know if that permission was subsequently received and when, if at all, the tapes were turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. We had a subsequent mission in April of 1998, and it was during that mission, late April, that -- that we were given permission to take those tapes and other materials with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the particular tape, Q2, was that among the tapes that was turned over in 1998, April?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know who was involved in the turning over of those tapes from the military end of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was the Q2 turned over singularly or turned over with other tapes. ?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was turned over with the other 19 tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Have you confirmed the circumstances of its transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have with the Court's permission, 65 ter 1069 on the e-court, please. Before we -- before we proceed, could you stop right there? I wanted to bring the Court's attention -- can we just go into private session for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just waiting for the document to appear in e-court. There it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, is this the document that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And were you able to confirm the circumstances of the transfer through examination of this particular document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. And I was there at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: -- also.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is and just so the record is clear, could you tell us what this particular document is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's a transfer, it's a receipt that the 2 Corps wrote up, handing over the 19 tapes to Jack Hunter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. It reflects a date of transfer of the 25th of April 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Were you able to confirm when the tape was received by the Evidence Unit following this particular transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The evidence log shows that the tapes came back to the ICTY in March of 2000 and that they were submitted into evidence in April, April 4th of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And have you subsequently had contact with the tapes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. At this point I would like to actually play the particular tape. I could proceed otherwise with respect to the second tape and then play them both with the Court's permission. I don't know how you would prefer to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can safely leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Then I guess at this point what I would like to do is play the tape in question. That's tape Q2. The tape has been, as I understand it, cued up and is ready to be played. It will be played on the original machine which has already been provided to the sound booth. And I would like to direct the Court's attention first to tab 2. And the counter for the record of the conversation is 082 to 095. I wonder if it would be possible, because I know that the tape is in B/C/S, I know that the Court has a transcript, but I don't know if it would be possible to even follow the conversation in English, listening to it in B/C/S. I wondered if it would be possible if Ms. Frease could direct the Court by using the ELMO as to what specific line the tape is referring to in English, if that would be of benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She's your witness. You proceed according to what you consider --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- conducive to the Prosecution. And if there is anything that the Defence objects to, we'll provide accordingly. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To me or to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, probably to you and the Prosecutor. Seems like on page 31 line 17 Mr. Vanderpuye says, "I would like to direct the Court's attention first to tab 2." I'm just curious if you have something we don't have. I don't have anything that has tab 2 on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tab 2 is a transcript. Tab 2 is a transcript of what allegedly is tape Q2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Nobody provided Defence counsel with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out. And I think we'll need to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could just bear with me for a moment. My understanding is that this was provided to Defence counsel actually before the turn of the year, in November at some point, because it specifically related to conversations that were the subject of testimony for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- operators that had come to court to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't solve anything. I don't think that Mr. Meek was intending to say that they had never been provided with this transcript. What's important is that this transcript is available now while Ms. Frease will be asked questions about it. I suppose one can download it straight on e-court. I would imagine. You have the ter number, the 65 ter number, which is 106 -- no. Q2 would be 1379. All right. There are copies available. We can make them -- who else from the Defence teams doesn't have a copy of the transcript of Q2?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour. Nobody on the Defence team has received that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're not contending that they were provided today. We're contending essentially they were provided a couple of months ago. I was under the impression - I do apologise - that it was pretty well understood that these tapes were going to be the subject of the testimony today. I know I didn't e-mail anybody in particular to say to bring the packet with you, but I'm not sure if the question is that you've never received -- the issue is that you've never received them or you just don't have them with you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau, I think it's very obvious, I don't think anyone needs to answer that question. They don't have it available now. So that's the position. And I think you are wasting time. We could have utilised the time to have them photocopied and brought in the courtroom in the meantime while we have been discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll see if I can have that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is as I understand it is one version -- one version is going to be on the ELMO, if I under Mr. Vanderpuye well. He's going to ask Ms. Frease to point out excerpts from it. The other one, the English version, can be put on the -- on e-court, and I see -- I see it there. And one can follow accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can proceed. [Microphone not activated]. It's 65 ter number PO1387E, for the record. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Whenever the -- whenever they're ready in the booth, we could play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could proceed to the second conversation, which is tab 3, for the benefit of the Court. And 65 ter 1396, for e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we stop it, please? I don't think it's on e-court yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still have the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let's start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I have the 65 ter number for the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 65 ter number for the B/C/S. I understand it's 1396C.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record that was tab 3, and the counter on the tape machine will run from 112 to 126. I'd like to proceed with the other tape, if I may, and continue doing direct examination. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you give the 65 ter number to Madam Registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's 1395F, that's the tape. If I may inquire, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, are you familiar with the tape that's designated T000-0822?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Is that otherwise known as tape number 49?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you know the circumstances under which that particular tape came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. It was obtained during a search of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina military archives in October of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And have you examined any material in order to confirm the circumstances of its transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally what that material was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: There was a -- a log that I looked at from the ICTY OTP team that seized the material, as well as a transcript from a witness that testified in the rebuttal case of the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what particular -- what particular parts of the transcript or documents you referred to in order to confirm the circumstances of this transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: There was one document that originated from 2 Corps in Tuzla that showed the transfer of 86, I believe it was, reel-to-reel tapes to their Sarajevo headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter number 1067, please displayed on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Ms. Frease. Is this the document that you had just referred to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And just so the record is clear, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a receipt from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 2 Corps headquarters, from their intelligence section, that is a record of various documents, archival material, tapes, audiocassettes, reel-to-reel tapes and others that were transferred to -- to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina's Main Staff, and the date on that document is September 19, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you review any other documents in relation to your confirming the circumstances of this transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Other than the testimony, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated something about a log; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, when you said transfer, I thought you meant transfer from 2 Corps to Sarajevo, but transfer from Sarajevo to the ICTY, yes, I did review other documents. And there was a log that -- there were two logs, actually. One that was produced by the Sarajevo intelligence department in which they provided a breakdown of the tape and the contents of that tape, very similar to the kind of breakdowns that we produced internally. And then the second log was a log of -- a record of the search that was conducted by a different OTP team in Sarajevo that was responsible for actually taking possession of that tape, among a large body of other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 1073, please, shown on e-court. First, if I could, the first page of it, and then the fourth page of it with an ERN ending 2485. Is this the document that you're referring -- okay. If we could just go back to the first page for a moment, please. Is this the document you were referring to concerning a log relating to the search of archives located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we please turn to page -- I think it was four. It's ERN ending 2485. Did you review this particular page in relation to this transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was a magnetic reel-to-reel tape designated number 49, among the tapes that were inventoried as a result of the search?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, can you tell us -- there are a number of rows here, can you tell us where that is --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- on this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: -- on the far left column, document number 100132, one page, and the date located 17 October of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And there is an indication --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: And there is an indication, exactly, that 98 audiomagnetic reels were seized and it provides the numbers of those reels; among the numbers is a tape number 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 1070, please, displayed on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It is an internal log that the military intelligence battalion for an electronic -- the electronic warfare company for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I guess at that time it was -- it was called the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina army, produced on the 1st of July, 1998. It relates to tape number 49 and provides a breakdown of the contents of that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to compare the contents as it is summarised on this document with the contents of tape T000-0822, both in terms of its contents and sequence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do they conform to one another?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would at this time like to have the tape played, and we can follow the same procedure as before. The first conversation is at tab 4. The P number is 02352E for the English version, the B/C/S version is -- P 02352F in B/C/S. For the people in the sound booth and for the record, the counter number should run from 016 to 025 on the UHER machine. I think whenever the sound people are ready we can play the tape. Is it in e-court? It's not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like if we could proceed to the next intercepted communication. That is 13 -- 65 ter 1387E, the English version, 1387F in B/C/S. For the record, for the people in the booth, the counter is 047 through 057. And for the Court's benefit, it's tab 5 of the packet. If you can tell me -- is it ready? Okay. Whenever the people are ready in the booth, I think we can begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is it possible to get the English versions on the e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I have. Now, if -- if -- oh, yeah, that's the ELMO, sorry. Yes. We have to change that. On e-court it's not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's the wrong number. Could you check the 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, if I could just ask you, do you know or are you able to verify or check where these particular conversations originally recorded, whether it was the northern facility or the southern facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's redact that, please. Just the name of the site we need to redact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, the -- you've indicated what we're listening to now originated in the southern site?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the -- and the previous tape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Originated in the northern site.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. I guess we're ready to go. And that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do we have -- you knew exactly what I was going to say. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check what appears in e-court is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not. It's definitely not. I mean, the one that appears -- that should appear should start with X, "momenat."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think it's 65 ter number 01387E.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That appears to be correct. Okay. If we're ready to play the tape, I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I would like to play the -- the last intercepted communication, which is 65 ter 1395E for the English version, and 65 ter 1395F for the B/C/S version. It's tab 6 for the Court's reference, and for the counter, it is 059 through 066. I just ask the people in the booth to wait until it's actually loaded into e-court before it's played. All right. Do we have the -- okay, we're ready. Any time you're ready in the booth, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point I would like to have the actual tapes brought into the courtroom and shown the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Frease, you have with you two boxes. And those contain the reel-to-reel tapes that you've testified about previously?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just start with the one that's on top, please?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think maybe it would be a good idea to place it on the ELMO, so that everybody can see what it is that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it possible to zoom out just a little bit? All right. We'll start with the cover. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you recognise that to be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The tape cover for tape Q2, what we used to call Q2, which is now T000-0471.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any designation of the -- well, of Q2 on the box? ?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. On the -- on the -- the side right here, just -- shall I try to turn it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Okay. And could you indicate, just pointing to it exactly where it is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be in the lower part of the side, or the back, spine, I should say --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- of the box?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you flip it over to the other side, the side that previously wasn't displayed, just so everybody can see what is on there. Now, would you be so kind as to open -- open the box, please. And could you place it back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The box?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there -- there appears to be an index on this portion, on the inner portion of the box.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It seems to refer to -- well, material that was previously recorded on this tape. One of the interpreters told me that this "Tuzla Slet - 83" probably referred to little dances that people were doing for Tito's birthday or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you turn that over to the other side, please, just so that everybody can see what it is? Okay. And that side of it is blank; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to remove the physical tape from the box? And place that on the ELMO. Okay. There's a label on that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that corresponds to the tape that was played, T000-0471?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that was the label put on by the ICTY's evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you turn this tape over, please, to the other side? Okay. On the lower part of the screen it's "48"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us -- well, could we just pull that a little bit, zoom out just a little? There's a designation on the top of this tape that appears to say Q48. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you able to determine whether or not this tape is the Q2 tape that was referred to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And how are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: By actually looking at the magnetic tape itself. Because when Jack Hunter, the expert from the ATF lab, first examined the 19 tapes in Tuzla in March of 1998 he wrote on the end close to where the actual magnetic tape began.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to find the designation Q2 on the lead to this tape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If it's possible, could you pull that out and show that on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Is this the designation you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that indicates a date of 3/11/98?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right. Which in American -- the way that we record dates in the U.S. it would mean March 11th, 1998, which was when Jack Hunter was at 2 Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And based on this, are you able to confirm that the tape was received by the evidence unit was the tape that was turned over to Jack Hunter?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're done with this tape. Okay. For the record, the -- this particular tape, T000-0471 corresponds with 65 ter number 1422. The tape in its entirety, okay. I would like you to take a look at the second tape, if you could. This tape should be T000-0822.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Do you want me it take it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like you first to put the cover on the ELMO so the Court can see. All right. Now, on this particular tape cover is the number 32.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any idea what that corresponds to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you turn it over, the tape? Okay. On the other side it is blank, of the cover, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you turn the tape on to its spine, please? Okay. And here there appears the designation T000-0822, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that corresponds to the -- the tape that you previously testified about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please open the box? Okay. And can you tell us what appears on the cover?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. It's an internal cover to the tape that has the number 39 on it, written in two different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, previously you had indicated that this particular tape was a tape number 49?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you able to verify that that is, in fact, the case with respect to this tape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Number 49 is written on the actual reel-to-reel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Is it possible to display that on the ELMO so that the Court can see what you're referring to? Okay. This is the actual tape, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Has a label that corresponds to T000-0822?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And there is an indication on this side of the tape of 49A?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that designation is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the log that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina provided, they indicated that tape 49, side A, didn't have any material on it. So I would say that this is side A of tape 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you turn the other side over, please? Okay. Can you tell us what's on -- what appears on this side of the tape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Also a number 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. There's no particular designation 49B?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But there is on the other side of the tape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I think I have no further questions at this point. Thank you, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Frease. I understood earlier on that you wanted to show us machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have the machines and, yes, I can show them to you, if you would like to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I understood Mr. McCloskey had said earlier on. I don't know how -- whether it is for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'll show it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: To the Court. Just a moment, before Ms. Frease leaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, I wanted to ask you about the machines because I see you did bring it with you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what you have there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's an UHER machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can that go on the ELMO? It seems kind of heavy, but maybe. Can we come out a little bit? That's as far as we can go? Okay. You say this is an UHER machine?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And are you familiar with the operation or use of these machines?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just describe to the Court how this machine is set up and what specific characteristics it has?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It has a -- it has a tape counter on it, it has controls to play, to start, to pause it, to stop it, to record, and to rewind and fast forward. It also has a knob where you can control the speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
